warmup.q: At closing time, a job prints the day's bill for every table, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Each table's task submits a fetch of that table's orders to the same pool and calls get() on it. With the 5 tables of a test, it takes 2 seconds. On a busy Saturday there are 400 tables. What happens?
options: It takes about 80 times longer, because the pool is busy
The pool grows past 20 threads to keep up
It hangs forever, with the CPU near zero
The JVM detects the deadlock and throws in one of the tasks
warmup.why: The first 20 bill tasks take every thread, and each one waits for a fetch that is queued behind 380 other bill tasks. No thread will ever be free to run a fetch, so the job hangs. A fixed pool never grows, and the JVM's deadlock detector looks for threads holding locks in a circle, not for tasks waiting on queued tasks, so nothing throws. The fourth section takes it apart.

opening:
Picture the kitchen on a Saturday night, when the orders stop coming out. Which cook is stuck? Every cook wears the same white jacket and no name tag. Which table was the burned dish for? The note with the table number stayed with the waiter. How long has the rail been this full? Nobody kept count. And at closing time, someone turns off the lights with two dishes still in the oven.

A thread pool, the team of threads that runs a program's tasks, meets the same questions, and its defaults answer none of them. Its threads are called pool-3-thread-7. A task sent with submit can fail without a word. The request's label stays on the thread that started the work. And shutdown() waits for nothing. None of this shows up in a test.

The last lesson split arithmetic among cooks who steal from each other, and this one runs pools for real. In this lesson, we'll add name tags, catch every failure, carry each request's note along, read the numbers that warn of trouble, untangle a pool that waits for itself, and close the kitchen in order. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a stuck kitchen and questions nobody could answer. Now each has an answer: name tags on every thread, one wrapper that reports every failure with its request id, a note that travels with the order, four numbers on the board, no cook waiting for a ticket behind him, and a closing routine that fits the deadline.

Now find where your own code creates pools, and give each one a named thread factory. Then search for .get() and .join() inside tasks, and check that none waits on its own pool.

Next, we'll start the virtual threads track with the thread-per-request wall. If every waiting request holds a costly platform thread, what happens when the requests outnumber the threads?

sections.h: Name tags and lost failures: naming threads, and catching what submit hides
sections.html:
A thread's name, its name tag, shows up in log lines, in profilers (tools that show where a program spends its time) and in thread dumps. A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread in a running JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs your program, with its name, its state and the line of code it is on. You can take one with jcmd <pid> Thread.print, where <pid> is the number the operating system gave the program.

The ready-made pools from Executors name their threads pool-3-thread-7, the seventh thread of the third pool. In a dump of a program with eight pools, that tells you nothing. A thread factory is the object a pool asks for each new thread. Hand the pool one that names its threads:

Java
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory();   // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ...
ExecutorService grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named);
Kotlin
val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory()            // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ...
val grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named)

Before JDK 21 (version 21 of Java's development kit), you write a small ThreadFactory of your own.

Now failures. The first lesson of this track showed that execute and submit treat a failing task in opposite ways. In production, that difference decides whether you ever hear about it.

FailureDemo, in the Try it below, makes a pool with one thread. The factory names it grill-0 and gives it an UncaughtExceptionHandler, the method the JVM calls when an exception escapes a thread. This one prints a line. Then it sends one failing task through each method. Predict what each half prints:

1. execute() a task that throws
  handler: grill-0 died of java.lang.IllegalStateException: the grill went out
   the next task runs on grill-1
2. submit() a task that throws
   (nothing printed) the next task runs on grill-1
   only get() shows it: java.lang.IllegalStateException: a negative price

With execute, the exception escaped the task. The worker grill-0 died, the handler ran, and the pool started grill-1 in its place. With submit, the FutureTask, the wrapper that submit puts around a task, caught the exception and kept it. Nothing printed, and grill-1 carried on. The grill going out at least made some noise. The negative price would have stayed quiet forever if the demo hadn't called get(). In fire-and-forget code, which hands over a task and never looks at its result, nobody does.

The default handler prints a stack trace to System.err, outside your logs and with no request id. So a handler on the thread factory covers only half the cases, and that half badly.

To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. submit, invokeAll and CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool) all end up calling execute. So a ThreadPoolExecutor subclass that overrides execute and wraps each task sees all of them.

The wrapper runs the task inside a try. A task from execute throws, and the catch reports it. A task from submit doesn't throw: it's a FutureTask, and after it runs, state() says FAILED and exceptionNow() (both JDK 19) hands over the original exception. Report it with the request id, and don't rethrow. Rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool, ProductionPool.

submit hides failures and execute kills workers. Report both from one wrapper.

That wrapper reports a request id, which raises a fair question: whose request id does a pool thread have?

try.title: Find out who hears about a failure
steps: Read FailureDemo. Its threads are named grill-N and have an UncaughtExceptionHandler.
Before you run it, predict for each case: does the handler print, and which thread runs the next task?

code.title: FailureDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadFactory; /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ public class FailureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ThreadFactory factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("grill-", 0) // grill-0, grill-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) -> System.out.println(" handler: " + t.getName() + " died of " + e)) .factory(); try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory)) { System.out.println("1. execute() a task that throws"); pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("the grill went out"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); System.out.println("2. submit() a task that throws"); Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("a negative price"); }); Thread.sleep(200); System.out.println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit(() -> Thread.currentThread().getName()).get()); try { f.get(); } catch (ExecutionException e) { System.out.println(" only get() shows it: " + e.getCause()); } } } }

alt.title: FailureDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.Executors /** Named threads with an UncaughtExceptionHandler. Which failures does the handler see? */ fun main() { val factory = Thread.ofPlatform() .name("grill-", 0) // grill-0, grill-1, ... .uncaughtExceptionHandler { t, e -> println(" handler: ${t.name} died of $e") } .factory() Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1, factory).use { pool -> println("1. execute() a task that throws") pool.execute { throw IllegalStateException("the grill went out") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) println("2. submit() a task that throws") val f = pool.submit<Unit> { throw IllegalStateException("a negative price") } Thread.sleep(200) println(" (nothing printed) the next task runs on " + pool.submit<String> { Thread.currentThread().name }.get()) try { f.get() } catch (e: ExecutionException) { println(" only get() shows it: ${e.cause}") } } }

try.expect: For execute, the handler prints grill-0 died of ... the grill went out, and the next task runs on grill-1: the pool replaced the dead worker. For submit, nothing prints, the next task still runs on grill-1, and the exception appears only when get() is called.

sections.h: The note pinned to the wrong jacket: carrying request context to the worker
sections.html:
A request id is a short label, such as req-42, that a program gives each request it handles and prints on every log line about it. Programs often keep it in a ThreadLocal: a variable that has a separate value for each thread, as Don't share: immutability, confinement, ThreadLocal showed. Any code on that thread can read it without passing it around.

The trouble starts at the hand-off. Picture a note about table 4, "nut allergy", pinned to the jacket of the waiter who took the order instead of clipped to the order itself. The order goes to the grill, and the note stays with the waiter. The grill cook sees no note at all. Or he still has an old note pinned to his own jacket, from the last order he cooked.

ContextDemo acts that out with a pool of one thread. main sets the request id to req-42, then submits three tasks. Predict all three lines:

1. plain task sees:   null
2. wrapped task sees: req-42
3. next task sees:    req-7  (left over from an earlier task)

Line 1 is the missing note: the pool's thread never saw req-42. Line 3 is the old note. An earlier task set req-7 on the worker and never removed it, and the next caller had no request id at all. Every log line from that task now blames request 7, which finished long ago and did nothing wrong.

Line 2 is the fix, in three steps. Capture the value on the submitting thread, install it on the worker before the task runs, and put the worker's old value back afterwards:

Java
static Runnable withRequestId(Runnable task) {
    String captured = RequestContext.get();            // 1. on the submitting thread
    return () -> {
        String previous = RequestContext.get();
        RequestContext.set(captured);                  // 2. on the worker
        try {
            task.run();
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous);   // 3. never leak
        }
    };
}
Kotlin
fun withRequestId(task: Runnable): Runnable {
    val captured = RequestContext.get()                // 1. on the submitting thread
    return Runnable {
        val previous = RequestContext.get()
        RequestContext.set(captured)                   // 2. on the worker
        try {
            task.run()
        } finally {
            if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous)   // 3. never leak
        }
    }
}

In the kitchen, that is copying the note onto the order ticket, pinning it on whichever cook cooks the dish, and taking it off when the dish leaves.

The capture must happen in the method that runs on the submitting thread, which is why it sits outside the lambda. Read the ThreadLocal inside the lambda instead, and you read the worker's value, which is the bug you set out to fix. The finally matters just as much. Pool threads are reused, so whatever a task leaves behind becomes the next task's context.

Here the picture breaks. A paper note falls off sooner or later. A ThreadLocal value stays on its thread until some code removes it.

Don't make every caller remember: wrap once, in the executor everyone uses, as the lab's ProductionPool does.

Virtual threads, the subject of the next track, don't change any of this: a new thread starts with empty ThreadLocals, except inheritable ones, which copy their value from the thread that starts them. Scoped values, final in JDK 25 (JEP 506, the design document behind them), are the newer tool for request context, and that track covers them too.

A ThreadLocal belongs to a thread, not to a task. Capture it at the hand-off, and clean up after.

Names, failures and context make one task easy to trace. The next question is about all of them at once: is the pool keeping up?

try.title: Lose a request id, then leak one
steps: Read ContextDemo. The main thread sets req-42 and submits three tasks to a pool with one thread.
Predict all three lines before you run it. For line 3, find the task that caused it.

code.title: ContextDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ public class ContextDemo { static final ThreadLocal<String> REQUEST_ID = new ThreadLocal<>(); // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up static Runnable withContext(Runnable task) { String captured = REQUEST_ID.get(); return () -> { String previous = REQUEST_ID.get(); REQUEST_ID.set(captured); try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) REQUEST_ID.remove(); else REQUEST_ID.set(previous); } }; } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1)) { REQUEST_ID.set("req-42"); pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("1. plain task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get())).get(); pool.submit(withContext(() -> System.out.println("2. wrapped task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get()))).get(); // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit(() -> REQUEST_ID.set("req-7")).get(); REQUEST_ID.remove(); // the next caller has no request pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("3. next task sees: " + REQUEST_ID.get() + " (left over from an earlier task)")).get(); } } }

alt.title: ContextDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.Executors private val requestId = ThreadLocal<String?>() // capture on the submitting thread, install on the worker, always clean up private fun withContext(task: () -> Unit): Runnable { val captured = requestId.get() return Runnable { val previous = requestId.get() requestId.set(captured) try { task() } finally { if (previous == null) requestId.remove() else requestId.set(previous) } } } /** A request id in a ThreadLocal, handed to a pool three ways. */ fun main() { Executors.newFixedThreadPool(1).use { pool -> requestId.set("req-42") pool.submit { println("1. plain task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }.get() pool.submit(withContext { println("2. wrapped task sees: ${requestId.get()}") }).get() // a task that sets the ThreadLocal itself and forgets to remove it pool.submit { requestId.set("req-7") }.get() requestId.remove() // the next caller has no request pool.submit { println("3. next task sees: ${requestId.get()} (left over from an earlier task)") }.get() } }

try.expect: Line 1 prints null: the plain task runs on a pool thread that never saw req-42. Line 2 prints req-42, because the wrapper captured it on main. Line 3 prints req-7, left over from the earlier task that set the ThreadLocal and never removed it, although the new caller had no request at all.

aside.title: What is an MDC, and why do log lines need it?
aside.html: If your program logs with SLF4J, a widely used logging library for Java, it has an MDC, short for Mapped Diagnostic Context. The MDC is a small map of values for the current thread, such as the request id, and the log format can print a value from it on every line. It is built on a ThreadLocal, so everything in this section applies to it. Frameworks for web services often put the request id into the MDC when a request arrives, on the thread that handles it. The lab's RequestContext is a one-value stand-in for it.

sections.h: The board by the pass: four numbers that show a pool falling behind
sections.html:
A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it's often the first place a slow service shows up. A good kitchen keeps a board by the pass, and four numbers on a pool's board tell you most of what you need.

The queue size, getQueue().size(), is the number of tickets on the rail. A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law, from Sizing a pool (tasks inside = arrival rate x time each one stays), says each task's wait grows with it.

The active count, getActiveCount(), compared with the maximum, says how many cooks are busy. A pool stuck at its maximum for minutes has no room left, and it's usually waiting on something further along the path, not working hard.

The rejections are the tasks the pool turned away. ThreadPoolExecutor doesn't count them for you. Wrap the RejectedExecutionHandler, the code a pool calls when it refuses a task (Inside ThreadPoolExecutor), in one that adds to a counter and then throws.

The time in queue is how long each task waited for a thread. The caller feels that wait, and the task never measures it. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts.

MetricsDemo sends a burst of 10 tasks of 300 ms each to a pool of 2 threads, named orders-, with a queue of 4 and a counting handler. Then it prints the board every 200 ms. Predict the first row before you read it:

  ms  threads  active  queued  done  rejected
   0        2       2       4     0         4
 244        2       2       4     0         4
 446        2       2       2     2         4
 647        2       2       0     4         4
 849        2       2       0     4         4
1050        2       0       0     6         4

Two tasks run, four wait in the queue, and four are rejected at once, since 2 + 4 = 6 is all the pool can hold. After that, every 300 ms two more finish. The queue goes 4, 2, 0, done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 at about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4, and those four callers heard the bad news at once instead of waiting for it.

Picture the same burst on newFixedThreadPool(2), whose queue has no limit. The board would show rejected 0 and a queue of 8. Every task is accepted, and the last two wait 1.2 seconds before a thread even picks them up. Only the time in queue would show the trouble. That's why it belongs on the board.

The getters are approximate, as their Javadoc, the official documentation, says, because the threads change the numbers while you read them. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. If your program already sends numbers to a dashboard, a metrics library such as Micrometer can read most of these from a pool for you.

Of the four, time in queue and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look.

Watch the queue, not just the threads. Count every rejection.

Now picture a board where every number has frozen: all threads active, the queue full and not moving, nothing done, and the CPU idle.

try.title: Read a pool's board
steps: MetricsDemo sends 10 tasks of 300 ms to a pool with 2 threads and a queue of 4. Predict how many are rejected, and when the queue empties.
Run it, and read the table row by row.

code.title: MetricsDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue; import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder; /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ public class MetricsDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws InterruptedException { LongAdder rejected = new LongAdder(); ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("orders-", 0).factory(), (task, executor) -> { rejected.increment(); // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw new RejectedExecutionException("orders pool full"); }); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { try { pool.execute(() -> sleep(300)); } catch (RejectedExecutionException e) { // the waiter would say "come back later" here } } System.out.println(" ms threads active queued done rejected"); long t0 = System.nanoTime(); for (int i = 0; i < 6; i++) { System.out.printf("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d%n", (System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.getPoolSize(), pool.getActiveCount(), pool.getQueue().size(), pool.getCompletedTaskCount(), rejected.sum()); sleep(200); } pool.shutdown(); pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); } static void sleep(long ms) { try { Thread.sleep(ms); } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } }

alt.title: MetricsDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.ArrayBlockingQueue import java.util.concurrent.RejectedExecutionException import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.atomic.LongAdder /** 10 tasks of 300 ms hit a pool of 2 threads with a queue of 4. Watch the numbers a dashboard would show. */ fun main() { val rejected = LongAdder() val pool = ThreadPoolExecutor(2, 2, 0, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS, ArrayBlockingQueue(4), Thread.ofPlatform().name("orders-", 0).factory()) { _, _ -> rejected.increment() // count it, then fail like AbortPolicy throw RejectedExecutionException("orders pool full") } repeat(10) { try { pool.execute { Thread.sleep(300) } } catch (e: RejectedExecutionException) { // the waiter would say "come back later" here } } println(" ms threads active queued done rejected") val t0 = System.nanoTime() repeat(6) { println("%4d %7d %6d %6d %4d %8d".format((System.nanoTime() - t0) / 1_000_000, pool.poolSize, pool.activeCount, pool.queue.size, pool.completedTaskCount, rejected.sum())) Thread.sleep(200) } pool.shutdown() pool.awaitTermination(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS) }

try.expect: Two tasks run, four wait in the queue, and four are rejected right away (2 + 4 = 6 accepted). Every 300 ms two more finish: the queue goes 4, 2, 0 while done climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and active drops to 0 after about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4.

sections.h: Cooks waiting for tickets behind them: pool-induced deadlock
sections.html:
At closing time, a job prints the day's bill for every table. For each table, a task fetches the table's order lines from the order book, a database, and then renders the bill. Someone split the fetch into a task of its own, on the same pool:

Java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> orders.lines(table));   // a task inside a task
    return render(table, lines.get());                                     // waits for it
});
Kotlin
pool.submit<String> {
    val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { orders.lines(table) }   // a task inside a task
    render(table, lines.get())                                     // waits for it
}

With 20 threads and the 5 tables of a test, it's fine. On a busy Saturday there are 400 tables. Let's trace it with those numbers.

  1. The first 20 bill tasks take all 20 threads.
  2. Each one submits its fetch, and the 20 fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 waiting bill tasks.
  3. Each bill task then waits in get() for its fetch.

Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. In the kitchen, every cook has taken a bill ticket, pinned a "fetch the orders" ticket at the back of the rail, and stands waiting for it. No cook is left to take the fetch tickets.

DeadlockDemo builds the smallest case: two bill tasks on a pool of two threads named bills-, where each fetch takes microseconds:

after 300 ms: active=2, queued=2, completed=0
no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start

Both threads are active, the two fetches are queued, and nothing has completed. Speed isn't the problem. The demo gives up after 2 seconds, but the pool would wait forever. This is pool-induced deadlock, which Java Concurrency in Practice calls thread starvation deadlock: every thread in a bounded pool, one with a fixed number of threads, waits for a task that is queued in that same pool.

Unlike the lock deadlock of Deadlock, livelock and starvation, the CPU drops to zero, nothing throws, and a thread dump has no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is simply WAITING in FutureTask.get. The figure shows the moment.

Here are three fixes, in the order I'd try them:

  1. Don't block inside the pool. Compose: supplyAsync(() -> orders.lines(t), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(t, lines)). The render step runs as a callback, code that runs when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end. The demo's fixed mode does this and prints both bills at once, on the same two threads.
  2. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the bill task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline, in the same task.
  3. Give each stage its own pool. Bill tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the bill pool. That's a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, a separate limit for each stage.

A cached pool, with no limit on threads, hides the hang by starting a thread for every waiting task, which moves the problem to memory and to the database. Calling join() inside a CompletableFuture stage is the same bug, which is why CompletableFuture: composing async steps warned against it.

No task may wait for another task in its own bounded pool. Compose, inline, or use a second pool.

Our pools can now run well all day. At night, they have to stop.

try.title: Hang a pool on purpose
steps: Run DeadlockDemo: two bill tasks on a pool of two threads, each waiting for a fast fetch on the same pool. Read the active and queued counts.
Run it with -Pargs=fixed, which composes the fetch and the render with CompletableFuture. Predict how long it takes.

code.title: DeadlockDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.executors.l09; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService; import java.util.concurrent.Executors; import java.util.concurrent.Future; import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException; /** Two bill tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ public class DeadlockDemo { static List<String> fetchLines(String table) { return List.of(table + "-1", table + "-2"); // fast: the problem isn't speed } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { boolean fixed = args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("fixed"); ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bills-", 0).factory()); try { if (fixed) { List<CompletableFuture<String>> bills = List.of("t1", "t2").stream() .map(t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchLines(t), pool) .thenApply(lines -> t + ": " + lines.size() + " lines")) // nobody waits inside the pool .toList(); bills.forEach(b -> System.out.println(b.join())); return; } List<Future<String>> bills = List.of("t1", "t2").stream() .map(t -> pool.submit(() -> { Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> fetchLines(t)); // queued behind us return t + ": " + lines.get().size() + " lines"; // waits for it })) .toList(); Thread.sleep(300); ThreadPoolExecutor tpe = (ThreadPoolExecutor) pool; System.out.printf("after 300 ms: active=%d, queued=%d, completed=%d%n", tpe.getActiveCount(), tpe.getQueue().size(), tpe.getCompletedTaskCount()); try { System.out.println(bills.get(0).get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)); } catch (TimeoutException e) { System.out.println("no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start"); } } finally { pool.shutdownNow(); // interrupts the stuck get() calls } } }

alt.title: DeadlockDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.executors.l09 import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture import java.util.concurrent.Executors import java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit import java.util.concurrent.TimeoutException private fun fetchLines(table: String) = listOf("$table-1", "$table-2") // fast: the problem isn't speed /** Two bill tasks on a 2-thread pool, each waiting for a fetch on the same pool. Pass "fixed" to compose instead. */ fun main(args: Array<String>) { val fixed = args.firstOrNull() == "fixed" val pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(2, Thread.ofPlatform().name("bills-", 0).factory()) try { if (fixed) { val bills = listOf("t1", "t2").map { t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ fetchLines(t) }, pool) .thenApply { lines -> "$t: ${lines.size} lines" } // nobody waits inside the pool } bills.forEach { println(it.join()) } return } val bills = listOf("t1", "t2").map { t -> pool.submit<String> { val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { fetchLines(t) } // queued behind us "$t: ${lines.get().size} lines" // waits for it } } Thread.sleep(300) val tpe = pool as ThreadPoolExecutor println("after 300 ms: active=${tpe.activeCount}, queued=${tpe.queue.size}, completed=${tpe.completedTaskCount}") try { println(bills[0].get(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) } catch (e: TimeoutException) { println("no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start") } } finally { pool.shutdownNow() // interrupts the stuck get() calls } }

try.expect: The default run shows active=2, queued=2, completed=0 after 300 ms, then gives up after 2 s with no bill, although each fetch takes microseconds. The fixed run prints both bills at once, on the same two threads.

sections.h: Closing the kitchen at night: shutting pools down in order, within one deadline
sections.html:
A good restaurant closes in a fixed order. First someone locks the front door to new guests. Then the kitchen finishes the orders it has, starting with the stations that feed the others. Only then do the lights go off, and all of it must fit before a deadline.

A program stops the same way. As the first lesson of this track described, the system that runs a service usually sends a polite signal first. After a grace period, 30 seconds by a common default, it stops the program by force. Everything in flight has to finish inside that window, or be written down as lost.

Here is a stop method for a program with two pools. The kitchen pool's tasks cook dishes, and each finished dish is handed to the billing pool, which adds it to the table's bill:

Java
void stop() throws InterruptedException {
    intake.stop();                                                      // 1. no new orders come in
    long deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20);   //    inside the 30 s grace period
    for (ExecutorService pool : List.of(kitchenPool, billingPool)) {    // 2. upstream first: kitchen feeds billing
        pool.shutdown();
        long left = Math.max(0, deadline - System.nanoTime());
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            List<Runnable> neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow();           // 3. interrupt what is still running
            log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size());    // 4. say what was lost
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
fun stop() {
    intake.stop()                                                       // 1. no new orders come in
    val deadline = System.nanoTime() + TimeUnit.SECONDS.toNanos(20)     //    inside the 30 s grace period
    for (pool in listOf(kitchenPool, billingPool)) {                    // 2. upstream first: kitchen feeds billing
        pool.shutdown()
        val left = maxOf(0L, deadline - System.nanoTime())
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(left, TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)) {
            val neverStarted = pool.shutdownNow()                       // 3. interrupt what is still running
            log.warn("{} tasks never started", neverStarted.size)       // 4. say what was lost
        }
    }
}

First we stop intake. In a web service, that means no longer accepting requests. Otherwise new work keeps arriving at pools that are trying to drain.

Then we shut the pools down upstream first: the pool that hands work to the other one goes first. Get it backwards, and shut down billingPool first. The dishes still cooking in kitchenPool then get a RejectedExecutionException when they try to add themselves to the bill. They were cooked and served and never billed, a free dinner nobody planned.

The whole sequence gets one deadline, shorter than the grace period, shared between the pools. When a pool misses it, shutdownNow() interrupts what is still running and returns the tasks that never started. Log them, with request ids if your wrapper keeps them, so somebody can run them again.

If your program runs inside a framework, it usually offers a hook that runs at shutdown, such as a method marked @PreDestroy, an annotation that means "run me before the program stops". Put this code there. Never leave a pool for the garbage collector, the JVM's memory cleaner, to clean up: its threads keep it alive.

Check yourself: why one shared 20-second deadline, instead of 20 seconds for each pool? (The waits add up. Two pools at 20 seconds each can take 40, and the program is stopped by force at 30, before the log.warn line can say what was lost.)

Stop intake first, then drain pools upstream first, all within one deadline.

Look back over the whole track for its limit. Every pool we sized, named and drained holds one platform thread, the ordinary kind that wraps a thread of the operating system, for each task that waits, and platform threads are costly. A pool of 200 threads stops at 200 waiting requests, however idle the CPU is.

compare.title: Carrying the MDC: an executor wrapper vs a coroutine context element

java.title: MdcExecutor.java (SLF4J)
java.html: static Executor withMdc(Executor delegate) { return task -> { Map<String, String> captured = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); // 1. on the submitting thread delegate.execute(() -> { Map<String, String> previous = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap(); if (captured != null) MDC.setContextMap(captured); else MDC.clear(); // 2. on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous != null) MDC.setContextMap(previous); else MDC.clear(); // 3. never leak } }); }; } CompletableFuture.runAsync(() -> bills.add(dish), withMdc(billingPool));

kotlin.title: MdcCoroutine.kt (kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j)
kotlin.html: // MDCContext() copies the MDC now and installs it every time the coroutine // runs, on whichever thread that is, then restores the thread's own MDC scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + MDCContext()) { bills.add(dish) delay(100) // may resume on another thread log.info("added") // the request id is still in the MDC } // the same idea for your own ThreadLocal scope.launch(Dispatchers.IO + requestId.asContextElement(value = "req-42")) { /* ... */ }

compare.note: The Java wrapper installs the context once, because a task stays on one thread from start to finish. A coroutine, Kotlin's own light task, can move to another thread every time it suspends, so a wrapper around the whole coroutine wouldn't be enough. MDCContext() and asContextElement are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread, and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. One trap: an MDC.put inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, because the element keeps reinstalling the map it captured. The kotlinx docs say to wrap the change in withContext(MDCContext()).

worked.title: Diagnose a bill job that stopped on a busy Saturday

steps.say: The closing-time bill job has printed nothing for 30 minutes, and the CPU is near zero. A thread dump (jcmd <pid> Thread.print) shows all 20 bills- threads at the same spot. Before reading on, say what they are waiting for.
steps.code:
"bills-3" #41 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
	- parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(...)
	at com.example.restaurant.BillJob.lambda$run$0(BillJob.java)
	...

steps.say: Every thread is inside a bill task, parked in FutureTask.get(), waiting for another task's result. The pool's board finishes the story: active=20, the queue at 380 and not moving, completed flat. The fetch tasks they wait for are in that queue, behind the other bill tasks, and they need a free thread that will never come. The dump has no "Found one Java-level deadlock" line, because the detector looks for threads holding locks in a circle, and a Future has no owner.
The fix is to stop holding a thread while waiting. Compose the fetch and the render, start every table's pipeline, and let only the job's own thread wait at the end.
steps.code: List<CompletableFuture<String>> bills = tables.stream() .map(t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orders.lines(t), pool) // 1. fetch on the pool .thenApply(lines -> render(t, lines))) // 2. render as a callback .toList(); return bills.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList(); // 3. only the caller waits

alt.html: val bills = tables.map { t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ orders.lines(t) }, pool) // 1. fetch on the pool .thenApply { lines -> render(t, lines) } // 2. render as a callback } return bills.map { it.join() } // 3. only the caller waits

steps.say: Then make the next bad night shorter. The bills- name tags already paid off: they showed at once which pool was stuck. Add the queue size and the oldest task's wait for this pool to the dashboard, with an alert, so a queue that stops moving wakes someone up within minutes.

lab.title: A production pool, and a bill job to untangle
steps: Meet the classes. ProductionPool is a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue, and you'll give it named threads, carried context and failure reports. RequestContext holds the current thread's request id in a ThreadLocal. FailureLog is where the pool reports a failed task. BillJob prints a bill for each table, and it hangs. Run the tests: all eight fail, and the two BillJob tests time out after 5 seconds. That is the deadlock.
Write ProductionPool.create: build the factory with Thread.ofPlatform().name(name + "-", 0).factory() and pass it to the private constructor, which already sets up the bounded queue.

Write ProductionPool.execute. Read RequestContext.get() first, on the calling thread. Then call super.execute with a lambda that saves the worker's own context, sets the captured id, runs the task, and restores the saved context in a finally.

Report failures inside that lambda: catch RuntimeException | Error from task.run() and report it without rethrowing. After run() returns, if the task is a Future whose state() is FAILED, report exceptionNow().
Fix BillJob.run: start a supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render) pipeline for every table, then join them all on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: Capture the id before super.execute. Inside the lambda you are already on the worker, where RequestContext.get() returns the worker's value.
task instanceof Future<?> f && f.state() == Future.State.FAILED (JDK 19+), then f.exceptionNow(), gives you the original exception, not an ExecutionException.
If reportsExecuteFailures sees the next task on orders-1, your wrapper rethrew: the worker died, and the pool replaced it.
The BillJob fix needs no second pool. A thenApply callback never holds a thread while it waits.

drill.title: A context-carrying executor from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate): every task runs with the RequestContext of the thread that called execute, and the worker's own value is restored afterwards. Then compare. Where did you read the context, and is the restore in a finally?

answer.title: Contexts.java
answer.html: static Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate) { return task -> { String captured = RequestContext.get(); // on the caller's thread delegate.execute(() -> { String previous = RequestContext.get(); RequestContext.set(captured); // on the worker try { task.run(); } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear(); else RequestContext.set(previous); } }); }; }

alt.title: Contexts.kt
alt.html: fun withRequestId(delegate: Executor) = Executor { task -> val captured = RequestContext.get() // on the caller's thread delegate.execute { val previous = RequestContext.get() RequestContext.set(captured) // on the worker try { task.run() } finally { if (previous == null) RequestContext.clear() else RequestContext.set(previous) } } }

recap: Name every pool's threads (Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory() on JDK 21+), so dumps and logs say which pool is stuck.
An UncaughtExceptionHandler only sees execute failures, and submit hides them in the Future. Wrap execute once to report both, with the request id.
ThreadLocal context such as a request id doesn't follow a task to a pool. Capture it at submission, install it in the worker, and restore it in finally.
Watch the queue size, the active count against the maximum, rejections and time in queue. Count rejections yourself, in the handler.

A task that blocks on another task in the same bounded pool can hang the pool forever. Compose instead, do the work inline, or give each stage its own pool. Shut down in order: intake first, then pools upstream first, within one deadline.
The limit: every pool here holds one costly platform thread for each waiting task, so the thread count caps how many requests can wait at once.

explain.prompt: A friend's closing-time bill job works with 5 tables and hangs with 400, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Explain what is happening and two ways to fix it.
explain.answer: Each table's task submits the fetch of its orders to the same pool and blocks on get(). With 400 tables, the first 20 tasks take every thread, and their fetches are queued behind the other 380 bill tasks. A fetch can only run on a free thread, and every thread is waiting for a fetch, so nothing ever finishes. The CPU is idle and nothing throws, because no lock is involved. One fix is to stop blocking inside the pool: start supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render) for each table, so rendering is a callback and only the job's own thread waits at the end. Another is to run the fetches on a separate pool, so the bill threads wait on a pool that never waits back on them. Simplest of all, if the bill task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline.

deeper.html:
Why is the JVM's deadlock detector silent? jcmd <pid> Thread.print (and ThreadMXBean.findDeadlockedThreads) look for cycles of threads that each hold a lock another one needs: monitors from synchronized, and ownable synchronizers such as ReentrantLock. A thread waiting in Future.get() parks on the future, which has no owner, so there is no cycle to find. Names and stack traces are your only tools, which is one more reason to name threads.

The ThreadPoolExecutor Javadoc shows a second way to catch failures: override the afterExecute hook, which runs on the worker after each task:

Java
@Override
protected void afterExecute(Runnable r, Throwable t) {
    super.afterExecute(r, t);
    if (t == null && r instanceof Future<?> f && f.isDone()) {
        try {
            f.get();
        } catch (CancellationException e) {
            t = e;
        } catch (ExecutionException e) {
            t = e.getCause();
        } catch (InterruptedException e) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
        }
    }
    if (t != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().getName(), t);
}
Kotlin
override fun afterExecute(r: Runnable, t: Throwable?) {
    super.afterExecute(r, t)
    var failure = t
    if (failure == null && r is Future<*> && r.isDone) {
        try {
            r.get()
        } catch (e: CancellationException) {
            failure = e
        } catch (e: ExecutionException) {
            failure = e.cause
        } catch (e: InterruptedException) {
            Thread.currentThread().interrupt()
        }
    }
    if (failure != null) log.error("task failed on {}", Thread.currentThread().name, failure)
}

It works, with two limits. It can't stop an execute failure from killing the worker, because the exception is rethrown after the hook runs. And it doesn't know the submitter's request id unless a wrapper stored it. That's why the lab wraps execute. Its sister hook, beforeExecute(Thread, Runnable), is the natural place to measure time in queue, and terminated() runs once, when the pool has fully stopped.
